final_answer:
antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, an evolutionary mechanism. when antibiotics are used, they kill susceptible bacteria, but resistant strains—those with genetic mutations or acquired resistance genes—survive. these resistant bacteria reproduce, passing on their resistance traits. over time, this leads to a population dominated by resistant strains.  

overprescription accelerates this process by increasing the frequency of antibiotic use. each use creates selective pressure, killing non-resistant bacteria and allowing resistant ones to thrive. excessive or unnecessary prescriptions (e.g., for viral infections) provide more opportunities for resistance to emerge and spread. incomplete treatment courses also allow bacteria to adapt, as partial exposure may select for resistance. this repeated exposure to antibiotics skews the evolutionary balance, favoring resistance more rapidly than it would naturally occur.
